motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of uncertainty quantification in machine learning models, particularly in the context of predictive uncertainty quantification. Traditional methods often focus on conditional expectations and are limited by the law label process. Tolerance intervals and sets, which offer probabilistic bounds on the range of values that a random variable may take, are crucial for risk assessment and model evaluation. These bounds are typically derived from i.i.d. data, but their properties—such as expected width and coverage—have been less explored. Previous works have shown that conformal prediction with polynomial-time wrappers can control the expected width but typically do not minimize it. This paper aims to control the expected width of coverage sets while achieving the desired coverage, thereby providing a more efficient and effective way to quantify and reduce predictive uncertainty. The significance of this research lies in its ability to improve the efficiency of uncertainty quantification, which is essential for building trust in models and evaluating their performance in practical applications.
idea: The paper introduces a novel approach to improve the efficiency of uncertainty quantification in machine learning models by controlling the expected width of coverage sets. The key innovation is the use of Bayesian quadrature to derive width-sketching algorithms, which are algorithms with guaranteed expected width. The paper proves a uniform upper bound on the width of a width-sketching algorithm and provides an instance where the width in expectation is twice as large as the optimal width. To address this limitation, the paper introduces the width-optimality notion and an approximate version termed mean-width optimality. This allows for the derivation of algorithms with the desired coverage while minimizing the mean width. The paper also provides a high-level perspective on the relationship between width-sketching algorithms and depth-sketching algorithms, showing that they provide complementary forms of coverage, and demonstrates the application of the framework to conformal prediction with Bayesian quadrature.
title: Risk control with Width-Sketching Algorithms
abstract: We introduce the notion of width-sketching algorithms, defined as algorithms with \emph{provably} bounded width (that is, probability of containing the randomness) for the induced coverage set. For algorithms that sketch the width, we prove a novel uniform upper bound and provide an instance where the width in expectation is twice as large as the optimal width. We then introduce the width-optimality notion and an approximate version termed mean-width optimality, which allows us to derive algorithms with the desired coverage while minimizing the mean width. We provide a high-level perspective on the relationship with depth-sketching algorithms, i.e., algorithms that sketch the depth of the induced sets with probability $1- \alpha$, and show that they provide complementary forms of coverage. Finally, we demonstrate the application of the framework to conformal prediction with Bayesian quadrature.

Experimental_Setup.name: Univariate Counterexample Analysis
Experimental_Setup.description: This experiment constructs a simple instance where a width-sketching algorithm does not achieve the desired width control. The setup involves a probability space with a random variable u(x) defined as follows: u(x) is a uniform distribution on the interval [0,1] for x < 0 and a uniform distribution on the interval [1,2] for x >= 0. The width of the interval is measured using the L^1 norm, and the experiment analyzes the expected width and the probability of containing the true value u(x) for different values of s (the number of leaves in the depth sketch). The purpose is to show that the expected width can be twice as large as the optimal width in some instances.

Experimental_Setup.name: Multivariate Counterexample Analysis
Experimental_Setup.description: This experiment extends the univariate counterexample to a multivariate setting, where the random variable u(x) is defined as a uniform distribution on a box in R^2. Specifically, u(x) is a box with volume 1 for x(x) <= 0 and another box with volume 1 for x(x) > 0. The width of the interval is measured using the L^1 norm, and the experiment analyzes the expected width for different values of d (the dimension) and s (the number of leaves in the depth sketch). The purpose is to demonstrate that width-sketching algorithms do not achieve optimality for arbitrary tolerances in the multivariate case.

Experimental_Setup.name: Width-Sketching Algorithm with Penalty
Experimental_Setup.description: This experiment demonstrates the construction and evaluation of a width-sketching algorithm with a width-sketching penalty. The algorithm takes a parameter delta as input and produces a tuple (g(x), C(x)) where g(x) is the empirical quantile of the depth sketch and C(x) is the convex set of all values that minimize the distance to a set of leaves of the depth sketch. The width-sketching penalty is defined as the difference between the desired depth and the desired coverage. The experiment evaluates the width and depth of the interval produced by the algorithm and compares it to the empirical quantile algorithm. The purpose is to show that the algorithm controls the width in a uniform sense while reducing the depth with high probability.

Experimental_Setup.name: Width-Sketching Algorithm for Convex Sets
Experimental_Setup.description: This experiment demonstrates the construction and evaluation of a width-sketching algorithm for convex sets of possible values of u(x). The algorithm reparameterizes the problem with a random variable v(x) and produces an interval [g(x), C(x)] as the predicted value and coverage set. The g(x) is selected as a point that minimizes the distance to a convex set of leaves of the depth sketch, and C(x) is the convex set of all values that minimize the distance to a convex set of leaves. The width and depth of the interval are evaluated for different values of delta and compared to the empirical quantile algorithm. The purpose is to show that the algorithm controls the width in a uniform sense for arbitrary tolerances delta and achieves optimal depth with probability 1 for sufficient n.

result.description: The table presents the expected width and the probability of containing the true value u(x) for a simple univariate instance where the width-sketching algorithm does not achieve the desired width control. The left part of the plot corresponds to the width of the interval C(x,delta) = {u(x)} for each s, while the right part corresponds to the probability of containing the true value u(x). The results show that the expected width can be twice as large as the optimal width in some instances.
notes: For simplicity, the possible values of u(x) are assumed to be in [0,1].
The probability of containing u(x) is computed with respect to the uniform distribution on the possible values of u(x).
